5.a: (1) Minimum subscription test — the issue of 200000 shares at 10 rupees raises only application money of 3 rupees per share at this stage, and the SEBI threshold of 90 percent of 2000000 rupees, that is 1800000 rupees, is not met, (2) Refund — application money on the 50000 rejected shares, 50000 times 3 rupees = 150000 rupees, goes back to those applicants, (3) Pro-rata ratio — 250000 applied shares against 200000 issued shares simplify to 4 is to 5, so each accepted applicant receives 4 shares for every 5 applied, (4) Adjustment — accepted applicants paid 750000 rupees on application while 600000 rupees is due on 200000 shares, so the excess 150000 rupees adjusts against the allotment money due, (5) Verdict — the decision violates the SEBI minimum subscription rule. A student who skips the minimum subscription check fails the evaluation competency.

(1) Flawed premise — the base year is not normal, because the one-time gain on selling a factory makes that year's net profit abnormally high, (2) Misread trend — later percentages below 100 may simply reflect a return to normal profitability rather than decline, (3) Correct practice — select a base year free of exceptional items before computing trend percentages. A wrong answer that agrees with the student shows inability to critique base-year selection and confuses one-time gains with recurring profit.

(1) Stance — refute the statement, because access to more data does not decide reliability, (2) Argument one — external analysis rests on audited statements verified by independent chartered accountants, while internal ones may be unaudited and open to window-dressing, (3) Argument two — external users apply standard Ind AS frameworks and industry benchmarks, while internal analysis stays firm-specific and non-comparable. A wrong answer agreeing with the statement equates more data access with more reliable conclusions, ignoring the quality assurance of audit and the comparability of standards.

(1) Stance — the statement is false, because a maturity of three months or less is necessary but not sufficient, (2) The missing criterion — the investment must also carry an insignificant risk of changes in value, (3) Counter-example — an equity share portfolio held for two months fails that test, since its market value can swing sharply within two months, (4) Further counter-example — a two-month bond of a distressed company fails on default risk, and share investments stay excluded unless in substance cash equivalents. A wrong answer that calls the three-month rule sufficient has memorised the maturity test but missed the dual criteria of maturity plus risk.
